newsitem.title: USA: Clinton backs protections on use of genetic testing. [CORRECTED 22:59 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Clinton backs protections on use of genetic testing. [CORRECTED 22:59 GMT]

text.p: President Clinton on Monday endorsed legislation to ban health plans from discriminating against people on the basis of their genetic background.

The legislation is designed to ensure that health plans do not use genetic information, such as a propensity to develop breast cancer or another disease, to refuse health coverage or to raise premiums.
It would also block health care plans from disclosing such data to health insurerers and others but would permit its use in biomedical research if approved by the federal government.

Clinton backed the legislation at a White House ceremony attended by Mary Jo Kahn, who said that despite her family history of breast cancer she was unwilling to be tested for fear that health coverage would be denied her daughters.
"Americans should never have to choose between saving their health insurance and taking tests that could save their lives," Clinton said.

The initiative, a modified version of legislation already introduced in Congress by Representative Louise Slaughter, a New York Democrat, was a far cry from Clinton's failed first-term effort to overhaul the U.S. health care system.

In announcing his support of Slaughter's bill, which has also been introduced in the Senate by Maine Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe, Clinton said that having failed to reform the system as a whole, he is now doing so piece by piece. (Corrects spelling of Snowe.)

"This kind of discrimination is more than wrong, it's a life-threatening abuse of a potentially life-saving discovery," he said. "It is a direct consequence of the fact that we are the only advanced country in the world that has chosen to finance the health care of our citizens through a private insurance system that is completely optional and does not cover everyone."
He added: "I tried to fix it once and took a lot of criticism. I'm not ashamed that I did. If I could fix it tomorrow, I'd fix it tomorrow."
White House officials said some Republicans would back the bill, including Sen. Bill Frist of Tennessee, a surgeon who chairs an influential Senate subcommittee on public health.

The White House said Clinton modified the Slaughter bill to make it explicitly state that genetic information cannot be disclosed to insurers, plan sponsors as well as other entities regulated by state insurance laws.
However, the bill would give the secretary of health and human services authority to decide when it would be appropriate to disclose genetic information, such as for biomedical research efforts.
The bill is designed to close loopholes in last year's Kennedy-Kassebaum law that made it easier for workers to take their health insurance with them when they change jobs.

That law, sponsored by Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts and former Republican Sen. Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas, did not prevent health plans in the individual market from denying coverage on the basis of genetic information.
It also did not ensure that premiums were not based on genetic information nor did it prevent health plans from disclosing the information.
